conflicts.versions: Lesson 2 draws a single bold DOWNWARD sugar arrow along the stem. Lesson 3 says phloem is bidirectional (source to sink, including up to the cob), while xylem is strictly upward. Lessons 5 and 8 say sugars move mainly or only downward to roots (Lesson 8 also names growing tips and fruits as sinks).

conflicts.fact: Whether water transport in xylem needs energy, and what drives it
conflicts.versions: Lesson 3 teaches that xylem transport is passive and needs no energy, and it also builds a Venn row on 'energy requirement (passive/active)', hinting that osmosis needs none. Lessons 6 and 7 introduce transpiration pull and cohesion-tension as the driver. Lesson 3's Explained says the key question is what force pulls water up, but Lesson 3 also cites the root cortex and osmosis as established in Lesson 2, while Lesson 2 never covers osmosis.

Lesson 3 says osmosis evidence came from Lesson 2 ('Lesson 2 evidence about osmosis'; 'as established in Lesson 2'). Lesson 2 is about resource entry and use points and a transport system, with no osmosis. Osmosis is first investigated in Lesson 4.

conflicts.fact: When the cumulative model began and what it contained
conflicts.versions: Lesson 1 starts the model with a whole-plant diagram with xylem lines and stomata. Lesson 2 calls the revised diagram the 'first cumulative transport model'. Lesson 3 produces 'the first version' (Model v.1). Lesson 7 says the model has been built 'since Lesson 4'. Lesson 5 says 'since Lesson 1'.

conflicts.fact: Experiment used for the dye uptake and when it was set up
conflicts.versions: Lesson 5 sets up celery or white carnation stalks in food dye. Lesson 6 retrieves 'celery/maize stems' cross-sections soaked in red/blue dye from Lesson 5 and says results are observed in stem cross-sections. Lesson 5 says its Lesson 6 results are on celery stalks, not maize.

conflicts.fact: Position of xylem and phloem in the stem
conflicts.versions: Lesson 5 says xylem is inner and phloem outer (and uses adaxial/abaxial). Lesson 3 only says xylem and phloem run side by side, with no stem position given. Lesson 5 also says in its Explained that maize is monocot with scattered bundles while using dicot stems for observation, and its model asks for ring cross-sections, which does not match the maize plant being modelled.

Lesson 5 attributes permanent wilting to xylem cavitation (air embolisms) from drought tension, and mentions root rot from waterlogging. Lesson 8 attributes death to guard cells failing to close stomata or to phloem compromise from drought stress. Lesson 4 says low soil water potential halts or reverses osmosis.

conflicts.fact: Four transpiration factors versus Lesson 8 mechanism; role of stomata and plant used
conflicts.versions: Lesson 6 says stomata are open for photosynthesis on a hot afternoon and that shade reduces light and temperature, while Lesson 8 says stomata 'need not open as wide' in shade and speaks of guard cells failing to close. Lesson 7 asks what opens stomata at 2 pm on a hot afternoon, treating heat as the opener.

conflicts.fact: Impossible plant height and potometer plant
conflicts.versions: Lesson 7 uses a '10-metre-tall maize plant' for the Kibwezi crop, which is unrealistic since maize is about 2-3 m tall. Lesson 7 also uses a bougainvillea or succulent for the potometer, and Lesson 3 describes a long path length in 'tall maize' without any number.

Lesson 8 Predict uses a mango tree near Mombasa, while the Observe phase and Overview use a eucalyptus near Kericho. Lesson 8 predict also says abundant fruit set above the girdle, but the Overview says the examples are eucalyptus (which does not bear fruit) and bean plants.

Lesson 1's Observe phase photograph C description says the visibly moist soil is around the maize in photograph A, but photograph C shows sukuma wiki. Lesson 4 adds saline soil as the cause of wilting near the riverbed, which Lesson 1 and Lesson 8 do not mention (Lesson 8 says only lower soil water potential).
